title: India: Colonial Rule, Independence & Partition
description: From the East India Company to freedom — how Britain came to rule India, life under the Raj, Indian resistance from the 1857 rebellion to Gandhi's nonviolent campaigns, the road to independence, and the tragedy and legacy of the 1947 Partition.

notes.heading: The East India Company and the British Takeover
notes.body: British rule in India began not with an army of invasion but with a business. The **East India Company**, founded in 1600, came to trade in spices, cotton and silk, setting up fortified trading posts at Madras, Bombay and Calcutta with the permission of the **Mughal emperors**. As Mughal power crumbled in the eighteenth century, the Company filled the vacuum. At the **Battle of Plassey (1757)**, Robert Clive's small Company army, helped by bribery and the betrayal of the Nawab of Bengal's own generals, won a victory that gave the Company control of Bengal — India's richest province. Using Indian tax revenues to pay its soldiers, the Company expanded for a century: defeating rival Indian states, forcing rulers into unequal treaties, and governing through a private army of mostly Indian soldiers called **sepoys**. India was drained of wealth — its famous textile industry was undercut by machine-made British cloth — while famine relief and development were neglected. By 1850 a trading company, answerable only to its shareholders, effectively ruled most of the subcontinent.

notes.heading: Life Under the Raj
notes.body: After 1858 India was ruled directly by the British Crown — the period known as the **Raj**. A tiny British elite governed hundreds of millions: the **Indian Civil Service**, the 'steel frame' of the Raj, had fewer than a thousand British officers at its height. British rule brought real changes — railways, telegraphs, canals, a unified legal system and English-language education — but these were built mainly to serve British trade and control, and Indians paid for them through taxes. Economic policy favoured Britain: India exported raw cotton and imported British cloth, and local industries withered. **Famines** killed millions in the late nineteenth century while official relief was limited. Racial inequality was built into daily life: Indians were excluded from senior jobs, and some clubs and railway carriages barred Indians entirely. Yet the Raj also unintentionally created its own opposition — English education spread ideas of rights and democracy, and the railways and press let Indians organise across the subcontinent for the first time. Many Indians served loyally in the British Indian Army, showing the relationship was complex, not simple hatred.

notes.heading: Indian Resistance: The 1857 Rebellion and After
notes.body: The greatest challenge to Company rule came in **1857**, with the uprising the British called the 'Indian Mutiny' and many Indians call the **First War of Independence**. It began among **sepoys** of the Company's army, angered by pay, religious insults and — the immediate spark — new rifle cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, offensive to Hindus and Muslims alike. The rebellion spread across northern India: sepoys seized **Delhi**, and fierce fighting followed at Cawnpore (Kanpur) and Lucknow. It took the British more than a year of brutal campaigning to crush it, with terrible reprisals on both sides. The consequences were huge: in **1858** the British government abolished the East India Company and took direct control, Queen Victoria promised to respect Indian religions, and the army was reorganised. Resistance continued in new forms — in **1885** educated Indians founded the **Indian National Congress** to press for greater rights, at first politely and constitutionally, while the **Muslim League** (1906) spoke for Muslim interests. The stage was set for a mass independence movement.

notes.heading: Gandhi and Nonviolent Resistance
notes.body: **Mohandas Gandhi** returned to India in 1915 after fighting for Indian rights in South Africa, and transformed the freedom struggle. His method was **satyagraha** — 'truth force' — nonviolent resistance: boycott, strike and peaceful disobedience of unjust laws, accepting punishment without hitting back. He urged Indians to spin their own cloth (**khadi**) and boycott British goods, reviving village industries and hitting British trade. The **Amritsar Massacre** of 1919, in which British troops under General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd in the Jallianwala Bagh gardens, killing around 379 people, turned millions of Indians against British rule for good. Gandhi's most famous protest was the **Salt March** of **1930**: he walked about 240 miles to the sea at Dandi and illegally made salt, defying the British tax on a necessity everyone used. Around 60,000 people were arrested in the campaign that followed, and the world's press made Gandhi a global figure. Later campaigns — the **Quit India** movement of 1942, launched while Britain fought Japan — kept up the pressure. Nonviolence made British violence look indefensible and gave ordinary Indians a way to resist without guns.

notes.heading: The Road to Independence
notes.body: By the 1930s British rule was becoming impossible to sustain. The **Government of India Act 1935** gave Indians elected provincial governments, but real power stayed with the British viceroy. The **Second World War** changed everything. Britain's Indian viceroy declared war on India's behalf in 1939 without consulting Indian leaders; Congress ministers resigned in protest. Over two million **Indian soldiers** volunteered to fight — the largest volunteer army in history — and many expected freedom in return. Gandhi's **Quit India** campaign of 1942 demanded the British leave at once; its leaders were jailed for the rest of the war. Meanwhile the **Muslim League**, led by **Muhammad Ali Jinnah**, grew rapidly by demanding a separate Muslim homeland, **Pakistan**, fearing that Muslims would be a permanent minority in a Hindu-majority independent India. By 1945 Britain was exhausted and nearly bankrupt, the new Labour government wanted out, and the Royal Indian Navy mutiny of 1946 showed Britain could no longer rely on Indian forces. Independence was coming — the only question was whether India would stay united or be divided.

notes.heading: Partition 1947: Borders, Migration and Human Cost
notes.body: Unable to agree a united India, Britain, Congress and the Muslim League accepted **partition**: the subcontinent would be divided into Hindu-majority **India** and Muslim-majority **Pakistan** (in two wings, East and West, 1,600 km apart). A British lawyer, **Cyril Radcliffe**, who had never been to India, was given barely five weeks to draw the new borders through the mixed provinces of **Punjab** and **Bengal**. Britain's last viceroy, **Lord Mountbatten**, brought independence forward to **14–15 August 1947**, and the boundary was announced only afterwards — millions did not know which country they were in. The result was one of the largest and most tragic migrations in history: around **10–15 million people** crossed the new borders — Muslims heading to Pakistan, Hindus and Sikhs to India — and terrible communal violence erupted, especially in Punjab, killing an estimated **one to two million** people. Trains arrived full of dead; families were separated; cities such as Delhi overflowed with refugees. Gandhi, heartbroken that India had been divided, was assassinated by a Hindu extremist in January 1948. The joy of freedom was inseparable from the trauma of Partition.

notes.heading: Legacy of Independence and Partition
notes.body: The legacy of 1947 still shapes South Asia. **India** became the world's largest democracy, keeping its independence constitution of 1950, while **Pakistan** alternated between elected governments and military rule; **East Pakistan** broke away after a war in **1971** to become **Bangladesh**. The borders drawn in 1947 left a permanent dispute over **Kashmir**, claimed by both countries, which has caused wars in 1947–48, 1965 and 1999 and remains dangerous today because both states are nuclear powers. Partition's memory still influences relations between Hindu, Muslim and Sikh communities, and millions of families carry its stories across generations. Economically, India has grown into a major world power, while its film, literature and food have global reach; millions of people of South Asian descent live in Britain, a lasting human link from the imperial era. Historians still debate key questions: could Partition have been avoided, was Britain's rushed withdrawal to blame for the violence, and how should Gandhi's methods be judged? Understanding this history helps explain the modern politics of a region home to more than a fifth of humanity.

flashcards.definition: The British trading company, founded in 1600, which gradually conquered and ruled much of India until the British Crown took direct control in 1858.
flashcards.example: Its victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 gave it control of Bengal, India's richest province.

flashcards.definition: An Indian soldier serving in the armies of the East India Company or the British Raj.
flashcards.example: The 1857 rebellion began when sepoys refused to use rifle cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat.

flashcards.definition: The period of direct British Crown rule over India, from 1858 to 1947.
flashcards.example: Under the Raj, a tiny British-run Indian Civil Service governed hundreds of millions of Indians.

flashcards.definition: The great uprising against Company rule, begun by sepoys and spreading across northern India; called the 'Indian Mutiny' by the British and the First War of Independence by many Indians.
flashcards.example: Rebels seized Delhi, and the fighting at Cawnpore and Lucknow lasted over a year before British rule was restored.

flashcards.definition: The political organisation founded in 1885 that became the main movement for Indian independence, later led by figures such as Gandhi and Nehru.
flashcards.example: Congress launched the Quit India movement in 1942, demanding that Britain leave immediately.

flashcards.definition: Gandhi's philosophy of nonviolent resistance — 'truth force' — using boycotts, strikes and peaceful law-breaking while accepting punishment without violence.
flashcards.example: Gandhi's boycott of British cloth and his homemade khadi spinning were satyagraha in action.

flashcards.definition: The killing of around 379 unarmed Indians by British troops under General Dyer at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, in April 1919.
flashcards.example: The massacre turned millions of previously loyal Indians against British rule for good.

flashcards.definition: Gandhi's 1930 protest march of about 240 miles to the sea at Dandi, where he illegally made salt in defiance of the British salt tax.
flashcards.example: The Salt March led to around 60,000 arrests and made Gandhi famous across the world.

flashcards.definition: Leader of the Muslim League who campaigned for a separate Muslim homeland and became the first leader of Pakistan in 1947.
flashcards.example: Jinnah argued that Muslims would be a permanent minority in a Hindu-majority united India.

flashcards.definition: The 1947 division of British India into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, causing mass migration and communal violence.
flashcards.example: Around 10–15 million people crossed the new borders, and an estimated one to two million were killed.

flashcards.definition: The border between India and Pakistan drawn in barely five weeks by Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never visited India, and revealed only after independence.
flashcards.example: The line split the provinces of Punjab and Bengal, leaving millions unsure which country they lived in.

flashcards.definition: The mountainous region disputed between India and Pakistan since 1947, the cause of several wars and still a flashpoint between the two nuclear-armed states.
flashcards.example: India and Pakistan fought over Kashmir in 1947–48, 1965 and 1999.

questions.stem: Which organisation originally conquered and ruled most of India on Britain's behalf?
choices: The British Army
The East India Company
The Indian Civil Service
The United Nations
questions.explanation: The East India Company, a private trading firm, used its own army and Indian tax revenues to take control of most of India after the Battle of Plassey in 1757. The British government only took direct control in 1858.

questions.stem: Why was the Battle of Plassey (1757) such an important turning point?
choices: It ended the Second World War in Asia
It gave the East India Company control of Bengal, whose tax revenues funded a century of expansion
It forced Britain to leave India immediately
It created the country of Pakistan
questions.explanation: Plassey handed the Company Bengal, India's richest province. Bengal's taxes paid the Company's army, letting it defeat rival Indian states piece by piece over the next hundred years.

questions.stem: What event in 1857 is called the 'Indian Mutiny' by the British and the 'First War of Independence' by many Indians?
choices: The Salt March
The Amritsar Massacre
The great rebellion that began among sepoys and spread across northern India
The founding of the Muslim League
questions.explanation: In 1857 sepoys rebelled over grievances including cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, and the uprising spread to Delhi, Cawnpore and Lucknow. The different names show how each side remembers it.

questions.stem: What was the most important political consequence of the 1857 rebellion?
choices: The East India Company was abolished and the British Crown took direct control of India
India became independent
Gandhi became leader of India
The railways were torn up
questions.explanation: In 1858 the British government ended Company rule and governed India directly — the period known as the Raj. Queen Victoria also promised to respect Indian religions, and the army was reorganised.

questions.stem: A historian writes: 'British rule in India brought benefits, but they were designed to serve Britain first.' Which evidence best supports this view?
choices: The railways and telegraphs were built mainly to move British goods and troops, and India exported raw cotton while importing British cloth
British rule had no effects on India at all
Indians were given equal access to all senior jobs in the civil service
Famines disappeared completely under British rule
questions.explanation: The railways, telegraphs and education system brought real change, but they primarily served British trade and control, while Indian industries withered and Indians were excluded from senior posts — supporting the historian's judgement.

choices: Armed rebellion against the British
Nonviolent resistance — boycott, strike and peaceful disobedience of unjust laws, accepting punishment without violence
Paying higher taxes to win British friendship
Moving the capital to a new city
questions.explanation: Satyagraha, or 'truth force', meant resisting injustice without violence: boycotting British goods, spinning homemade cloth and breaking unjust laws peacefully. It gave ordinary Indians a way to resist and made British violence look indefensible.

questions.stem: What happened at Amritsar in April 1919?
choices: Gandhi was born there
British troops under General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, killing around 379 people
India and Pakistan signed a peace treaty
The East India Company was founded
questions.explanation: The Amritsar Massacre saw British troops shoot into a peaceful crowd trapped in the Jallianwala Bagh gardens. The killings destroyed much of India's remaining trust in British justice and fuelled the independence movement.

questions.stem: Why was the Salt March of 1930 such a clever choice of protest?
choices: Salt was a necessity taxed by the British and used by everyone, so breaking the salt law was a simple act that millions could copy — and it attracted worldwide attention
Salt was extremely valuable and made India rich
It was the only law Gandhi was allowed to break
It forced the British to leave India within a month
questions.explanation: The salt tax hit rich and poor alike, so defying it united all Indians in one easy act of disobedience. The 240-mile march, the illegal salt-making and the 60,000 arrests made headlines around the world and embarrassed Britain.

questions.stem: Why did the Second World War speed up Indian independence?
choices: The war had no effect on India
Britain was exhausted and nearly bankrupt by 1945, over two million Indian soldiers had fought expecting freedom, and Britain could no longer rely on Indian forces to hold India down
The war made Britain richer and stronger
India declared war on Britain
questions.explanation: The war drained Britain's money and will to keep the empire, while Indian wartime service strengthened the case for freedom. The 1946 Royal Indian Navy mutiny showed Britain could no longer count on Indian forces, and the new Labour government chose to leave.

questions.stem: Why did Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League demand a separate state of Pakistan?
choices: They wanted to keep British rule forever
They feared Muslims would be a permanent minority in a Hindu-majority independent India
They wanted to join the Soviet Union
They opposed independence altogether
questions.explanation: Jinnah argued that in a single democratic India, Muslims — roughly a quarter of the population — would always be outvoted by the Hindu majority. The Muslim League's campaign for a separate homeland made Partition almost unavoidable by 1947.

questions.stem: When did India and Pakistan become independent?
choices: August 1947
questions.explanation: Pakistan and India became independent on 14 and 15 August 1947. 1857 was the rebellion, 1919 the Amritsar Massacre, and 1971 the year East Pakistan became Bangladesh.

questions.stem: Why did the drawing of the Partition borders cause such chaos?
choices: Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited India, had barely five weeks to draw the line, and it was revealed only after independence — millions did not know which country they were in
The borders were drawn a decade before independence
The borders followed rivers exactly
No one crossed the new borders
questions.explanation: Radcliffe was given five weeks and no local knowledge to divide Punjab and Bengal, and Mountbatten delayed publishing the boundary until after independence day. Communities were split overnight, helping trigger panic, flight and violence.

questions.stem: What was the human cost of Partition?
choices: A few hundred people moved house
Around 10–15 million people crossed the new borders and an estimated one to two million were killed in communal violence
Nobody was affected at all
Only soldiers were killed, in a single battle
questions.explanation: Partition caused one of the largest migrations in history: Muslims fled to Pakistan, Hindus and Sikhs to India, and terrible violence — especially in Punjab — killed an estimated one to two million people.

questions.stem: Which long-term consequences of Partition still affect South Asia today?
choices: The dispute over Kashmir, wars between India and Pakistan, and the creation of Bangladesh in 1971
The return of the East India Company
The reunification of India and Pakistan in 1965
British rule being restored in 1980
questions.explanation: The 1947 settlement left Kashmir disputed between two nuclear-armed rivals, caused wars in 1947–48, 1965 and 1999, and broke apart in 1971 when East Pakistan became Bangladesh — consequences still shaping the region.

questions.stem: Why do many historians judge Britain's rushed withdrawal in 1947 to be partly to blame for the Partition violence?
choices: The hurried timetable, delayed border announcement and lack of preparation left millions vulnerable to panic and violence
Britain stayed too long in India
Britain built too many railways
Britain held too many elections
questions.explanation: Mountbatten brought independence forward, Radcliffe had weeks not years to draw the borders, and the boundary was revealed only after the handover. Historians argue a slower, better-prepared transfer might have reduced the chaos and bloodshed.
